#6632. New Orleans Guide: Where to Stay, Eat, Drink, and Revel in the Big Easy

A bastion of hedonism, New Orleans is where indulgence is expected, revelry encouraged, and a good time all but guaranteed. Without question, eating and drinking is part and parcel of any visit to the Big Easy—but the city’s culture extends far beyond beignets and Sazeracs, converting first-time visitors into lifelong devotees of its countless charms. All it takes is a stroll down its oak-lined avenues to spark a love affair with New Orleans. It happened to me—and over a decade later I’m still hypnotized, returning to the Crescent City year after year to get my fix.

For centuries, New Orleans has played host to literary giants and jazz luminaries, civil rights leaders, and iconic artists. It’s a mysterious place where funerals become parades, Voodoo is still practiced, and tombs are above ground. Adding to its uniqueness, the city winds along the Mississippi River and is surrounded by wetland habitats of swamps, bayous, and marshes.

The oldest neighborhood here is the French Quarter (also known as Vieux Carré), which despite its reputation for rowdy tourists and souvenir shops, is tightly woven into the tapestry of New Orleans culture (read: don’t skip it). But you shouldn’t stop there—the Marigny, Bywater, Tremé, Garden District, Bayou St. John, Freret, and Algiers Point (among others) should also be on your radar when curating an itinerary.

Whether you’re planning a first-time visit or returning for an annual pilgrimage, laissez les bon temps rouler with the ultimate New Orleans travel guide below.

Experiencing New Orleans by foot is quintessential. Thanks to flat terrain, compact neighborhoods, and several pedestrian-friendly streets, it ranks high in walkability. If you plan to use the streetcar to get around (another great option relied upon by tourists and locals alike), download the Le Pass app to search for schedules and purchase your ticket ahead of time. (If you don’t, be sure to bring exact change—$1.25—with you.) There are five different streetcar lines, the historic, open-air Saint Charles Line being the most charming (more on that ahead). Rideshares like Lyft and Uber are also available in New Orleans.

The best time to visit New Orleans depends on your travel goals. If pleasant weather is your prerogative, spring and fall will both be cool and comfortable. For those eager to join Mardi Gras festivities, late winter will be your best bet, whereas if you prefer the spooky vibes, October can’t be beat. For die-hard cocktail lovers willing to brave the heat, come in July when Tales of the Cocktail takes place. And if you’re keen to see the city festooned in lights and garlands, come for the holiday season.

You can almost imagine what it felt like to stroll through its glamorous halls when The Pontchartrain Hotel originally opened its doors in 1927. This Garden District icon (which began as a luxury apartment building but converted to a hotel in the ‘40s) clutches onto its nostalgic charm with details like the lobby’s original terrazzo floor, heavy velvet drapes, and gleaming crystal chandeliers. (Not to mention the hotel key cabinet behind the front desk.) The original owners allowed long-term guests to haul in their own furniture and decor, and that pied-à-terre flair lingers throughout the suites and guest rooms. There are four food and beverage spaces in the hotel: the Hot-Tin Rooftop Bar, their fine dining concept Jack Rose, The Silver Whistle Café, and the Bayou Bar for Creole-inspired dishes and live jazz. Previous guests include Truman Capote, Frank Sinatra, The Doors, and Tennessee Williams, who worked on A Streetcar Named Desire during his residency here.

Located in the Marigny (the French Quarter’s quieter, calmer neighbor), this boutique property from Ash Hotels is set within a former Catholic church that was erected in the 19th century. The rooms (each individually decorated) stretch across three different historic buildings: the schoolhouse, the rectory, and the convent. (There’s also the brick church next door with its stained glass windows and restored murals that is now used as an event space.) This is no doubt an aesthete’s hotel—there are over 700 antiques throughout the expertly curated spaces, as well as furnishings produced locally. (Don’t miss the cypress double staircase by the front desk; it will take your breath away.) From limestone clawfoot tubs, sumptuous canopy beds, and perfectly mismatched upholstery, a stay at Hotel Peter and Paul is right in step with what makes New Orleans a destination with distinction.

For those naysayers who profess they’ll never stay overnight in the boisterous French Quarter, The Celestine has other plans for you. This 14-room boutique hotel strikes a fetching balance between modern creature comforts and old-world charm (think: antiques and four-poster beds puzzled together with Dr. Vranjes toiletries and a curated wet bar)—and the interior courtyard set to the gurgling tunes of its three-tier fountain offers a slowed-down pace to immerse in the old city. The building dates back to 1791 and was once the home of Antoine Amédée Peychaud (founder of Peychaud’s bitters, father of the Sazerac cocktail) and his wife, Celestine. Tennessee Williams also stayed here when he was working on A Streetcar Named Desire in the 1940s, and his former suite has been converted into the hotel’s lobby. While here, don’t miss out on Peychaud’s Bar, where guests and passersby alike can enjoy a reserve cocktail dreamt up by Neal Bodenheimer from Cure Co.

If it wasn’t already obvious, the hotel scene in New Orleans is one of the very best in the country. But if you find yourself strolling along the city’s sidewalks, admiring the Queen Anne architecture of the Garden District, or the Creole cottages throughout The Bywater, a stay with Dear Valentine offers the best of both worlds. Founder Melissa Shelton snapped up a collection of homes throughout the city—each with architectural and historical significance—collaborating with conservationists, interior designers, and local artisans to create a compelling brand. On a recent visit, I stayed at Dear Valentine’s Bouligny Victorian property uptown. The imaginative design by Logan Killen Interiors made each day feel like opening the door to a jewel box (a very large, two-story jewel box), and the private backyard with a plunge pool offered respite after hours of walking. Thoughtful touches—keyless locks, a washer and dryer, and a massive chef’s kitchen—felt like home. But with the option to add on a private chef, grocery delivery, or a concierge, hotel-caliber services are also at your fingertips. Dear Valentine homes range in size and can accommodate between 4 and 42 people, making it an obvious pick for group travel.

As with so many historic hotels in New Orleans, Columns has toggled through several previous lives—first as a private residence, then as a boarding house during World War I, and finally as a hotel (which is now listed on the National Register of Historic Places). Locals know and love Columns for its massive porch—which becomes particularly lively during weekend brunch—and the interiors retain that private residence feel for guests, from toile wallpaper and stone fireplaces to a mahogany staircase that climbs upwards to reveal a stained-glass skylight. When you’re hungry (and thirsty), head for the bar (or garden) for a cocktail, followed by dinner at the restaurant helmed by executive chef Paul Terrebonne.

This 14-room boutique hotel tucked in the heart of the leafy Garden District is brought to you by local hospitality veterans, LeBlanc + Smith. The first thing you’ll notice upon arrival is the structure—it’s housed within a 19th-century mansion that’s been painted a shadowy slate blue. Similarly, the walls in the interior public spaces are tinted in deep jewel tones and decorated with a textural mix of clever antiques (e.g., a wood-carved birdcage) and vintage objects. There’s an all-day restaurant with both indoor and outdoor seating (the focaccia with goat cheese and olive oil is a must), a stylish lobby bar where you can pull up a stool or take your cocktail out onto the front porch, and out back, you’ll find a pool with an adjacent bar serving up small bites and tropical drinks.

A grand dame of New Orleans, this magnificent property opened its doors in 1893 as the Grunewald Hotel, eventually coming to bear its current moniker in honor of former president Theodore Roosevelt in 1923. Stepping into the gilded, block-long lobby with its soaring ceilings and 1867-era Eugène Farcot clock, guests are ushered back in time. Dive deeper into the hotel’s history with a visit to The Sazerac Bar, an iconic watering hole from the 1940s with well-preserved Art Deco design. Also not to be missed: the extensive salumi menu at the property’s Domenica restaurant, plus a bit of pampering at the Waldorf Astoria Spa (complete with a glass of welcome Champagne).

Well positioned within the Warehouse District, this elegant hotel (formerly Maison de la Luz) was built in the early 1900s and served as an annex to New Orleans's former city hall. Now, it’s one of the most admired boutique guesthouses in the city, offering 67 rooms. A nightly wine and cheese hour offers the opportunity to enjoy the ground-level lounge, which resembles the parlor of a well-traveled collector. (There’s also an honor bar for whipping up your own Sazerac or French 75). Stroll through to the next room, and you’ll discover the Instagram-ready breakfast nook with its blue-and-white wallpaper and towering windows. When you’re ready for a drink, slip into Salon Salon for a craft cocktail and small bites (I recommend the pommes pavé), or opt for an even more intimate setting in the guest-only speakeasy-themed bar, accessible via a bookcase door.

Despite being a city largely defined by its waterways, there aren’t a lot of hotels in the Crescent City that showcase views of the Mississippi River. Thankfully, Four Seasons Hotel New Orleans does—and quite magnificently so. The property sits along the riverbanks and soars four hundred feet into the sky, crescendoing at a 34th-floor observation deck. Among its many highlights are the rooftop swimming pool, as well as the circular Chandelier Bar in the lobby that sits beneath a glittering installation of more than 15,000 crystals (if you’re here on a Thursday, there’s live jazz from 6 to 9 p.m.). Enjoy a dinner at the property’s Miss River restaurant helmed by Chef Alon Shaya—the sweet potato brioche bread service is a must, as is the carved buttermilk-fried chicken for the table. As for accommodations, nothing beats watching Steamboat Natchez gliding by from the hotel’s gorgeous river-view suites.

New Orleans is a city abundant in historic mansions. And if you’re determined to sleep in one, I suggest you make it The Whit. This new opening on Prytania Street offers 15 rooms and suites and was named for Walt Whitman. (The poet’s three-month stay in the spring of 1848 significantly shaped “Leaves of Grass.”) The exterior of the Greek Revival mansion is imposing and impressive, guarded by palms, live oaks, and a magnificent Magnolia tree. The hotel was developed by Gretchen Trauth, who tapped Logan Killen Interiors for the design, and a team of specialists to preserve and restore original details—like the crown molding, which, for me, resembles frosting layers on an extravagant cake. Neal Bodenheimer developed the drinks program and features tableside punches, while Brechtel Hospitality oversees the culinary experience. (I cannot stress enough how crucial it is you order the seasonal scone for breakfast.) And for couples looking for somewhere romantic to tie the knot, The Whit has positioned itself as a wedding venue with dedicated bridal suites and construction on an iron-and-glass pavilion currently underway.

Among the oldest hotels in New Orleans, this 1885 Beaux-Arts landmark is one of the city’s crown jewels. Slipping past the doors (attended to by friendly bellhops) is like stepping back in time, where coffered ceilings, sparkly chandeliers, marble floors, and a wood-carved grandfather clock greet guests. Several important authors throughout history have written about the property, thus its designation as a literary landmark, and its suites are dedicated to legends such as Truman Capote and Ernest Hemingway. Hotel Monteleone’s pièce de résistance is the Carousel Bar on the ground level, which has been rotating and serving up drinks since 1949. Securing a seat at the 24-person bar is a feat, but guests can join an early access experience with the hotel’s renowned mixologist, Marvin Allen, who regales imbibers with tales of the bar’s storied past.

It’s the facade that first grabs your attention at Hotel Saint Vincent—two levels of ornate ironwork, with a red brick edifice rising handsomely from behind. The Lower Garden District landmark first opened in 1861 as an infant asylum, funded by an Irish philanthropist named Margaret Haughery. Much later, after a complete renovation, the hotel was unveiled in 2021. The interiors by Lambert McGuire Design strike a balance between nostalgia and modernity: teak chairs sit in dialogue with vintage Murano glass chandeliers, which cast light on custom Voutsa wallpaper in a psychedelic pattern. This interplay between texture, color, and shape weaves throughout all of the hotel’s spaces, including San Lorenzo and Paradise Lounge (the seasonal Italian restaurant and lobby bar) and a moody bar named Chapel Club. Order a spritz by the pool beneath the green scalloped umbrellas, or pop into the ByGeorge boutique for an embroidered Bode shirt or locally crafted candle before retiring to one of the 75 guest rooms and suites.

The Warbler made its anticipated debut in October 2024 along St. Charles Avenue, and with it arrived Mildred’s, a martini bar and restaurant worthy of any New Orleans travel itinerary. Much like the rest of the hotel, the interiors evoke the relaxed mood of a European café, but with a colorful New Orleans twist. The menu leans in the direction of Spain and was developed in partnership with CureCo and Andrew Zimmerman of Chicago's Michelin-starred Sepia. Kick off the evening with the vermouth service, followed by a specialty martini (there are eight to choose from) paired with clam toast encrusted with garlic and Calabrian chiles.

Blink and you might miss the entrance to Patula, but that would be a shame. This new all-day cafe and wine bar is cozied away in Krewe’s courtyard, and has rapidly become a favorite among locals and visitors alike. Chef Rob Tabone is among the cast of characters revitalizing the French Quarter’s dining scene, working hand-in-hand with local farmers and purveyors to curate a menu worth singing praises about. The wine list is equally distinct, with bottles coming from small producers focused on low-intervention winemaking.

You can’t discuss the modern craft cocktail movement in New Orleans without paying tribute to Cure. Neal Bodenheimer’s beloved spot on Freret Street—opened in 2009—is now one of the most celebrated bars in the country, with accolades including a James Beard Award and multiple inclusions on 50 Best. Despite all the clout, the atmosphere at Cure is relaxed and convivial, anchored by an imposing bar and ceiling-to-floor windows. A warning: Choosing your libation will prove challenging. The rotating cocktail list is packed with mind-bending flavors and combinations that are created in collaboration with Cure’s talented team of bartenders.

Tucked inside a former pharmacy from the early 1900s, this fine dining restaurant first opened in 1982 and was named after a Louisiana-born socialite who was the muse for painter John Singer Sargent's controversial Portrait of Madame X. Executive Chef Rob Mistry’s menu reflects his global upbringing—born in New York City, raised between suburban Paris and North Carolina, and a child of Parsi parents from Mumbai. You can expect regional New Orleans ingredients, but through Mistry’s sharp point of view. The blue crab toast with sambar and cucumber—served on Japanese milk bread—is worth booking a visit to New Orleans for alone.

Allow me to introduce you to your new favorite spot to slurp down briny oysters: Holywater has arrived in the French Quarter. If the name sounds familiar, that’s because there’s already a successful Holywater outpost in New York City. But its Louisiana counterpart is distinctly its own. The three-story restaurant is family-run and sits within an 1800s maritime chandlery, attired in nautical decor aplenty. Begin the evening with an order of the caviar tater tots and super-chilled wedge salad, followed by a tower of their oysters, shrimp cocktail, and crab dip.

Opened in June 2025, this contemporary Asian restaurant by Chef Ashwin Vilkhu is a love letter to family dinners from his childhood growing up in New Orleans. The Farouki Farouki interiors are inspired by golden hour in his family’s home where he learned to cook, and the restaurant is named after the street his family lived on after they moved from New Delhi to New Orleans in the 1980s. The four-course dinner takes guests on a sensory tour of his most cherished flavors, including the crab, brie, and Champagne soup, which pairs beautifully with a crémant.

For an easygoing snack and drink, head for Bar Pomona in the Marigny. The interiors read like a countryside diner (in the best way), and on Mondays they serve up lasagna alongside natural wines from regions such as the Jura and Savoie.

If you’re not already a tiki cocktail convert, this is the place to try it. The founder, Jeff Berry, is credited with reviving vintage tiki cocktails to their original glory in the 1990s, and the menu weaves together premium spirits with compelling flavors like anise, pandan leaf extract, and almond.

This breakfast, lunch, and weekend brunch spot is close to plenty of city highlights—like Audubon Park and Magazine Street shopping—but it’s a destination in its own right. The breezy interiors and natural light make perching in a corner by the window (dressed in gingham drapes) feel especially cozy. And with dishes like the grits carbonara and huevos rotos, it’s all too easy to find yourself at Cafe Malou multiple times in one New Orleans trip.

Rightfully earning its position on The New York Times’s 2024 Best New Restaurants list, this seafood-driven Mexican spot in the Bywater neighborhood is in a league of its own. Co-owned by sisters and Mexico City natives Ana and Lydia Castro (the former a James Beard Award-nominated chef), Acamaya is one of the most exciting new additions to New Orleans’s storied hospitality scene. There’s no point giving ordering advice here—everything on the menu is just that good.

Complement a morning in City Park with a leisurely lunch at Ralph’s on the Park. Guests can tuck into white cornmeal fried oysters and a plate of shrimp & grits while gazing out at historic live oaks. If you’re lucky, you’ll meet Arthur, the restaurant’s charming-as-ever maître d’.

Caribbean flavors meet Cuban heritage at this French Quarter mainstay that’s helmed by executive chef Alfredo Nogueira. The bar has been open for over a decade, but each visit offers something new thanks to its seasonal approach to ingredients. The cocktail menu is sensational (first-timers should get the classic Hurricane & Table), and flavorful dishes like the sweet plantains and fish rundown complement each other from start to finish.

A New Orleans fine dining classic, Brennan’s has been an institution since opening in 1946. The restaurant is credited with inventing the flaming dessert, Bananas Foster, which is theatrically prepared tableside and worth a visit for alone (though it’s worth mentioning the Eggs St. Charles on the brunch menu are to die for).

This quiet, snug restaurant in the lower French Quarter taps into Executive Chef Tom Branighan’s childhood in Southern Louisiana, while remaining anchored in French technique. Don’t be fooled by the pleasantly unpretentious atmosphere; the food here is serious. On a recent dine, I feasted upon braised celery hearts and tuna crudo wrapped around blue crab claw meat, paired with a Riesling curated by sommelier Molly Wismeier.

Perched on a quiet corner along Magazine Street, this uptown restaurant sits in a 19th-century building that once sold provisions like butter, fresh cream, and imported teas. The menu is helmed by James Beard Award-winning Chef Justin Devillier and offers a creative, contemporary spin on traditional New Orleans cuisine. Whatever you do, don’t leave without trying the blue crab beignets.

There are few culinary experiences in New Orleans more stimulating than the tasting menu at Emeril’s. Celebrity Chef Emeril Lagasse opened the flagship restaurant in 1990 and it’s now deftly guided by his son E.J. Lagasse. Expect it all—a lavish butter cart, Petrossian caviar, the finest and freshest Louisiana meats and produce—all savored within an elegant dining room designed with floor-to-ceiling glass that showcases the kitchen in its entirety, which you get a mini tour of at the beginning of your evening. (Might we suggest opting for the wine pairing with your tasting menu?)

There’s no such thing as the best po’boy in the city—there are too many fine contenders, each offering their own standout style. While Liuzza’s by the Track, Domilise’s, and Parkway Bakery & Tavern are worthy shout-outs for this Louisiana classic, Verti Marte is an undeniable top pick. Don’t expect to be seated—this is a cash-only deli in the French Quarter. But what it lacks in table space, it more than makes up for in flavor.

This modern Senegalese tasting menu—which was named the best new restaurant in the country at the James Beard Awards in 2024—was born from Chef Serigne Mbaye’s memories of growing up in Senegal. Many of the courses are served family style (a nod to West African dining traditions), and the menu draws a focus on seafood and produce from local farmers in South Louisiana. The menu changes often, but expect highlights like soupe kandja, a Senegalese okra gumbo soup with Gulf crab, palm oil, and Louisiana rice.

Named America’s Best New Restaurant by Bon Appétit in 2017, this humble sandwich shop continues to live up to its accolades. Hopefully you’re not on a diet: the fried bologna—which includes potato chips inside the sandwich—is a must-order, as is the frozen margarita, which is prepared with Cointreau, Squirt, and Mountain Dew.

Ask any local what that turquoise-and-white Victorian building in the Garden District is, and they’ll know instantly—it’s Commander’s Palace. Since 1893, this landmark restaurant has been serving up classic Creole classics such as turtle soup au sherry and Creole gumbo. Book a table on Saturday or Sunday for the lively jazz brunch.

Spend enough time in New Orleans, and you’ll become acquainted with the grand dame restaurants of the city—Arnaud’s being one of them. This family-operated restaurant is over 100 years old, has a jazz brunch, a killer ‘shrimp Arnaud’ dish, a bar dedicated to the French 75 cocktail, and flaming table-side service for their delicious Café Brûlot for two. (Tip: Ask about their secret Mardi Gras Museum.)

Right in the heart of Jackson Square yet somehow hidden in plain sight, this new raw bar is one of the most exciting recent openings in the French Quarter. Fives is in a National Historic Landmark building that dates back to 1851, and the design centers around a wooden horseshoe-shaped bar installed beneath a striking antique chandelier. It’s the kind of peaceful spot you can quickly pop into for a half dozen oysters and a glass of bubbles… but find yourself lingering around for the beef tartare and curated martini menu.

Tourist haven it may be, a pillowy beignet and a cup of chicory coffee is a must when you’re in New Orleans—don’t question it! If you’re not up for the wait at the original location, there’s an outpost in City Park that’s just as lovely.

Sylvain is a low-key (but reliably good) Southern bistro in the French Quarter that serves up crowd favorites like cast iron cornbread and slow-cooked short rib. If you’re here for brunch, the Champagne & Fries menu is an obvious go-to.

Need a romantic date night spot serving natural wines and French classics like escargot and bouillabaisse? Head for this tried-and-true spot in the Bywater. (Request a table in the garden out back for extra romance.)

Known and adored for both their warm muffulettas and refreshing Pimm’s Cup, Napoleon House is always worth a pitstop. It sits within a 1791-era building that was once inhabited by the mayor of New Orleans, and would go on to become a restaurant and bar by the Impastato family who emigrated from the Sicilian town of Cinisi.

Told through the lens of Latin, Southeast Asian, Indian, and other global flavors, the culinary narrative of Mister Mao is one that’s eclectic, lively, and unapologetically fun. The restaurant—decorated in the spirit of the tropics—is led by Chef Sophina Uong (who is Cambodian-American) and dishes range from an Indonesian fruit salad to addictive garlic noodles.

The Friday lunch at Galatoire’s might require men to wear jackets, but the occasion is anything but stuffy. The 1905-era dining room is less of a traditional restaurant experience and more of an immersive event. Lunch customers are known to stay for hours upon hours, sipping on signature Pimm’s cups and feasting upon shrimp remoulade and crabmeat au gratin. Adding to the fun: a brass band marches between the tables throughout the day, with diners following behind, napkins waving in the air.

This New Orleans-based eyewear brand’s French Quarter flagship on Royal Street is ideal for picking up a new pair of sunnies while in town. Stick around long enough and they may even offer you a glass of frosé from their in-store frosé machine.

Located within the former convent at Hotel Peter and Paul, this petite shop offers a fun mix of vintage clothes, stylish giftables, artisan jewelry, home goods, and more. Iris 1956 Founder Candias Smith curated the assortment, and it even includes items from the hotel, including the robes, bath line, and custom candles.

Since opening their doors in 2016, Pilot & Powell co-owners Kathryn Bullock Joyner and Coeli Hilferty Boron have been Nola’s resource for approachable luxury. Harmoniously blending brands like Totême, Bernadette, and Rochas, this Magazine Street store is where to go when you need a new wardrobe hero.

Die-hard vintage enthusiasts shouldn’t miss out on this Lower Garden District shop, which sources rare garments from several eras in fashion all around the world (everything from ethereal 1930s chiffon gowns to Moschino and Miu Miu). The owner modeled her brick-and-mortar after the great boutiques and salons of Paris, catching the attention of shoppers such as Blake Lively and Dita Von Teese along the way.

Head for Kentucky Street in the Bywater for this “unusual New Orleans culinary antiques shop” hawking everything from gorgeous copper cookware to brass bar carts. Or perhaps you’re after a French 19th-century hand-blown verre à café? This is the place to come and get lost in history.

If antique and vintage shopping is a priority, don’t miss Merchant House. And even if you’re not searching for something specific, this destination in the Lower Garden District is brimming with one-of-a-kind finds—in both fashion and interiors—to help you bring a piece of New Orleans back home with you.

Much more than a bookstore, this Black-owned independent company (named after writer James Baldwin) donates hundreds of books to impoverished communities, all in service to its mission of nurturing communities through the written word. On any given day, visitors can shop from the extensive assortment of titles by Black writers, sit in on an author talk, and spark up a dialogue with fellow book lovers at their cafe.

Hop aboard a flat-bottomed boat with Cajun Encounters to glide through the wild Honey Island Swamp. The company arranges pick-ups and drop-offs from several points throughout New Orleans, and it takes about an hour to arrive in gator territory. If you prefer a swifter speed, book a tour with Airboat Adventures to explore 20,000 acres of cypress swamps.

Often cited as the birthplace of jazz, this open space in the southern corner of Louis Armstrong Park is the site where enslaved people of color gathered on Sunday afternoons during the 18th and 19th centuries. It’s here that enslaved Africans drummed, danced, sang, and traded, with some of these gatherings numbering as many as 500 to 600 people. Born from these cultural expressions gradually came Mardi Gras Indian traditions, the Second Line, and eventually New Orleans jazz as we know it today.

Arguably the best World War II museum in the world, this comprehensive collection tells the story of the war that changed the world through impressive multimedia experiences, immersive exhibits, and an eye-popping number of artifacts and first-person detail. Be prepared to spend several hours here (if not the entire day) and don’t miss the 4-D experience narrated by Tom Hanks titled ‘Beyond All Boundaries.’

Take a spin on Steamboat Natchez—the last authentic steamboat cruising the Mississippi River. Jazz cruises are set to the tune of live musicians and an atmospheric narration by the captain. Learn about the history of the river while enjoying a bag of freshly-popped corn and a classic cocktail. And don’t miss the pre-sail pipe organ, which is powered by the steamboat’s massive boilers. Debbie Fagnano has played on the instrument since 1989, and concerts typically take place three times a day before cruises (10:30 a.m., 1:45 p.m., and 5:30 p.m.).

Often billed as the best way to see the city, New Orleans streetcars are as charming as they are convenient. If you have a free morning, grab a latte and pastry from Lagniappe Bakehouse & Coffee and hop on the St. Charles Streetcar to ride up its namesake avenue to admire the architecture and historic oak trees. (Tip: download the ‘Le Pass’ app ahead of time to buy your ticket, and simply show your screen to the conductor upon boarding. Otherwise, it’s $1.25 per ride and exact change only.)

If you’re visiting City Park, tack on an extra hour for a self-guided ride on a Surrey bike. Pedal around the lake and beneath one of the largest collections of mature live oaks in the world (including the iconic McDonogh Oak). You can even opt for a night ride, which is quite magical during the holiday season when the trees are lit up with over one million lights.

Take yourself on a self-guided walking tour of this elegant neighborhood, brimming with architectural significance. Whether it's a Greek Revival mansion once owned by Anne Rice or the three-story Italianate property where Mark Twain used to party, behind every iron gate lies a story worth untangling.

Housed in the oldest building in the Mississippi River Valley and one of the few remaining structures built during the French rule (reminder: most buildings in the French Quarter were constructed during the Spanish occupation), this convent was completed in 1752 and offers a fascinating look back in time through the lens of the Ursuline nuns who braved a five-month voyage on the Atlantic Ocean to run a hospital and educate young girls.

It would be sacrilegious to visit New Orleans and skip out on jazz. But where to begin? Frenchmen Street is always a strong bet—walk along the three short blocks and go where your ears take you (Snug Harbor, The Spotted Cat, and Blue Nile are all solid picks). Preservation Hall opened its doors in 1961 and offers intimate 45-minute sets every night, while Tipitina’s uptown is standing-room-only and known for its high energy. And for donation-based and knock-your-socks-off kind of jazz, head to Bayou Bar inside The Pontchartrain Hotel for their weekly programming.

New Orleans is a community that doesn’t shy away from the supernatural—it’s part of their daily vernacular. Understandably, the city’s many historic cemeteries play an integral role in its cultural identity, with many offering guides or the opportunity to explore alone. If you’re a first-timer, begin with a tour at the city’s oldest cemetery, St. Louis No. 1, where Marie Laveau is buried.

While the sculpture garden in City Park is indeed well worth a visit, for an off-the-beaten-path experience, head for Couturie Forest on the northern side of the park. This hidden gem offers several walking trails that wind through wetlands and woodlands, which are especially hospitable to birders (it’s considered the city’s top bird-watching destination).

This strange (and at times, macabre) collection of artifacts pertaining to the history of pharmacy and medicine sits within a classic Creole townhouse in the French Quarter. Step inside and you’ll be immediately transported back to the 19th and early 20th century, surrounded by old stethoscopes, opium bottles, and even irradiated face powder (remember when beauty products were radioactive?)

Rent a stand-up paddleboard or go on a kayak tour on Bayou St. John for a view of this historic neighborhood from one of the city’s most historic waterways. Keep an eye out for turtles and egrets, and sneak a peek at Park Island—a little-known area with mid-century modern architecture like the famed Ashtray House.

If your visit coincides with a particularly humid day, beat the heat with some time by the pool. Day passes at both The Blackbird Hotel and The Garden District Hotel are available to non-guests, with the latter offering a swim-up bar and in-water loungers. If you’re near the Bywater, The Country Club (famed for its drag brunch) also offers day passes for its pool.

These two historic homes in the French Quarter—one Federal style, the other Italianate—are managed by a nonprofit and are open for tours that examine the lives of the owners and enslaved people who lived on property. During the fall months, Gallier House offers a tour that focuses on Creole death and mourning rituals, while over at Hermann-Grima, visitors are guided through urban enslavement during 19th-century New Orleans.

Magazine Street may be celebrated for its antique shops and fashion boutiques, but it is also home to the Great American Alligator Museum, where you’ll enter a reptile skeptic and leave a gator enthusiast. The front of the building is a shop selling assorted souvenirs (ornaments with gators dressed as Santa Claus, pencils with alligator-shaped erasers, and so on)—while in the back lies a tiny museum packed with artifacts, taxidermy, and memorabilia. There’s even a small alligator swimming around in a tank, and fossils dating back 70 million years.

#6631. This Is the Best Way to Use Leftover Canned Pumpkin

Half a can of pumpkin leftover pumpkin may not be enough for another pie, but you can definitely put it to use in other fall recipes.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

Fall baking has a way of leaving you with awkward amounts of leftover canned pumpkin. So many recipes call for half a can or some other quantity that leaves you wondering what exactly you’re supposed to do with the rest. You put the open can of Libby’s pumpkin puree in the refrigerator with every intention of using it, yet a few days later, there it is, still waiting for you to come up with a plan. It’s not as though you can make half a pumpkin pie.

Fortunately, you don’t need much pumpkin to make something wonderful. In fact, one of the best things I’ve made with leftover pumpkin requires less than a cup, a handful of pantry staples and very little effort. It’s the sort of recipe that makes having leftover pumpkin feel less like a nuisance and more like a stroke of good luck.

These are a little different from the dense, chewy blondies you might be accustomed to. They have golden edges and a wonderfully soft, almost cakey center, thanks in part to the pumpkin puree. Brown sugar gives them their rich, buttery sweetness, while cinnamon and pumpkin pie spice make them taste unmistakably like fall. The recipe lists the chocolate chips as optional, though I’d argue strongly in favor of including them. Chocolate and pumpkin are excellent together, and the little pockets of melted chocolate are delicious against all those warm spices.

The pumpkin blondies also almost suspiciously easy to make. Everything comes together in one bowl, using ingredients you probably already have on hand. There’s no frosting to fuss with, no dough to chill and no pie crust to negotiate. Just spread the batter into a 9-inch pan and bake it for 25 to 30 minutes. You’ll have a dozen soft, spiced bars that are equally at home on a Thanksgiving dessert table as they are next to your morning coffee.

Best of all, the recipe calls for just 1/2 cup of canned pumpkin. That’s a particularly convenient amount when you’ve got the remains of another baking project taking up residence in the refrigerator. And if you have a full cup left, making a double batch seems like a perfectly reasonable course of action.

And there’s no reason to limit pumpkin to sweet recipes. A few spoonfuls can add body and richness to soups, pasta dishes and risotto, especially when paired with sage, garlic and Parmesan. Just be sure you’re using plain pumpkin puree rather than pumpkin pie filling, which already contains sugar and spices and isn’t as versatile.

If you’re not quite ready to commit to another pumpkin project, you can always freeze your leftover pumpkin puree. That way, the next time a recipe calls for an odd amount of pumpkin, you’ll have some on hand.

#6629. How We Brought a Taste of Maine to Bon Appétit LIVE

Attendees of Bon Appétit Live experienced a taste of Maine through a hands-on lobster cooking class and a demonstration of wild blueberry cornmeal shortcakes, both hosted by Visit Maine.

The class, Lobster 101, was led by Bon Appétit manager of audience strategy Carly Westerfield and Krista Tripp, founder of Aphrodite Oysters in South Thomaston, Maine. Attendees learned how to break down a whole, steamed two-pound Maine lobster and transform the meat into a rich, creamy lobster dip—ideal for holiday hosting. Guests then enjoyed the fruits of their labor, sampling the freshly made dip with Ritz crackers before tasting oysters.

Tripp explained that her oysters, cultivated in the cold tidal waters of the Lower Weskeag River, take three years to reach maturity. Known for their distinctive fluted shells, they offer a briny, mineral-rich flavor balanced by a mellow sweetness.

After years as a lobster harvester, Tripp started Aphrodite Oysters to diversify her lobster business and has since shifted her focus to oyster cultivation full-time. She’s come to appreciate the many environmental benefits of farming and consuming them. Her oysters filter up to 50 gallons of water a day, taking in nitrogen and sequestering some for their growing shells. “Eating an oyster is contributing to the environment,” she declared. Indeed, water test scores have improved at her farm, demonstrating that bivalves help create a healthier ecosystem.

Before the end of the class, a few brave attendees volunteered to shuck their first oysters. Krista guided them through the process, demonstrating how to safely do it at home by protecting the hand holding the shellfish with a towel and gently working the knife into the hinge until the shell released. The well-earned reward was another taste of the Penobscot Bay, as fresh and pristine as the waters themselves.

Later in the day, guests in the Demo Kitchen were treated to Cornmeal Shortcakes with Blueberry Compote, prepared by Bon Appétit senior Test Kitchen editor Jesse Szewczyk. The compote featured wild Maine blueberries from Brodis Blueberries, a multigenerational family farm in Hope, Maine, stewarded by Ron Howard and his family. Howard joined Szewczyk for the demo, where he shared that 99% of the wild blueberries grown and harvested in the United States come from Maine. Attendees learned that they have been growing since the end of the Ice Age, when the tenacious plants, fortified by ericoid mycorrhizal fungi, began to grow and colonize the newly exposed land as glaciers retreated. An important food source for Native Americans, wild blueberries were valued by Indigenous communities for their nutritional benefits well before the modern superfood movement.

Speaking passionately, Howard discussed the many challenges facing Maine growers, including tariffs and currency exchange fluctuations, particularly the impact of a stronger Canadian dollar. Like many Maine farmers, the family has had to get creative. Howard invested in new equipment, including a more efficient type of harvester that allowed the business to scale up and sell to retailers. They created a shelf-stable, freeze-dried product with no added ingredients, allowing them to ship their product beyond the local area. Howard and his son started a distillery, where they use wild blueberries to make an eau de vie and vodka. They have also begun hosting a Wild Blueberry Weekend, opening the doors to the farm and educating the public about the unique benefits of their crop and their growing process.

Carolann Ouellette, director of the Maine Office of Tourism, emphasized that visiting Maine and engaging with local growers and producers such as Howard and Tripp was the best way to experience the state’s diverse bounty. “The relationship between people and nature is inseparable, and stewardship is an important part of the state's identity,” she reflected. Ouellette grew up in New Jersey but relocated to Maine over 40 years ago. Her family used to visit Maine when she was a child, and she recalls those experiences vividly: “As a kid, I remember, when you get to Maine, you can smell the pie or smell the spruce.” It’s those potent memories that drew her to the state permanently, a place she described as “filled with hardworking, welcoming communities that depend on one another.”

A few years ago, Visit Maine began placing greater emphasis on the state’s culinary identity. Ouellette said that awareness of Maine as a food destination continues to grow, “Sea to table with local ingredients is what we were doing before it was a thing.” Beyond the lobster, Visit Maine has been intentional about showcasing the breadth of the state’s agricultural, fishing, and heritage industries. Apples, potatoes, kelp, seaweed, and grains are just a few of the local ingredients featured in Visit Maine’s newsletter and Bountiful Plate video series, which highlights food and beverage producers throughout the state. Ouellette noted that Maine’s food culture is more diverse than many people expect, and its abundance of local products has attracted an interesting mix of exceptional chefs, many of whom are deeply embedded in their communities. Ouellette cited Tripp’s practice of personally delivering her oysters to local restaurants as an example of how the hospitality ecosystem is interconnected.

Most important, Ouellette emphasized that sustainability and stewardship are central to the state’s approach to its food systems and relationship with the landscape. “You can’t get much fresher than food in Maine,” she concluded.

Bon Appétit LIVE 2026 was sponsored by East Fork, Visit Maine, and S.Pellegrino® Sparkling Natural Mineral Water with thanks to All-Clad, As Ever, Bachan’s, Better Sour, Field Company, Floura, Gimme Seaweed, GOODLES, Graza, Hedley & Bennett, Kann Coffee, Material Kitchen, Misen, Owala®, Rip Van, SharkNinja, and Staub.

#6628. Turkeytini

When you're wrapping up Thanksgiving dinner, you're probably looking for a tasty drink and a little something sweet to finish the meal. But why not have both at the same time with a dessert cocktail? This boozy Turkeytini has all you need to complete your Thanksgiving feast with the decadent blend of creamy Baileys Irish cream, chocolate liqueur, Kahlúa, and bourbon.

Hot tip: Make sure to shake the cocktail for a good 20 seconds or more to get it homogeneous and frothy. This is the secret to getting a smooth drink without any curdling or separation. This recipe makes one drink, but feel free to increase all the ingredients to make a big batch—plus, the more Reese's, the better!

The garnish:It's entirely optional, but I took a note from our Oreo turkeys and made an adorable Reese's turkey as a garnish for this drink. Here's how you do it: Dot the back of 2 candy eyes with melted chocolate. Place on a Reese’s Thins cup. Use more chocolate to attach the orange part of a candy corn as the beak. For feathers, halve another cup and attach to the back with more chocolate. I promise it will make your drink all the more delicious (and adorable).

#6627. Chicken Broccoli Alfredo

Recipe by LaDonna Reed, Ponca City, Oklahoma

It takes just 25 minutes to make chicken broccoli Alfredo by combining veggies and meat in a creamy garlic and Parmesan sauce.

I love dishes that make it feel like you’re treating the family to a dinner at a restaurant, and anything with Alfredo definitely falls into that category. And yet, even though the cream sauce in this chicken broccoli Alfredo is made from scratch, it’s actually totally doable at home. (Plus there’s no need to dress up to go out to eat—you can enjoy this meal in your pajamas if you want to!)

There are a lot of ways to adapt this chicken Alfredo recipe using up other ingredients you might have on hand. Make it with chicken breasts as written, or swap in chicken thighs or leftover rotisserie chicken instead. Use fresh broccoli or pull those frozen florets from the freezer. Spice up the Parmesan sauce with a little extra cayenne pepper, or add a swirl of herby pesto.

Cook the fettuccine according to the package directions for al dente. Add the broccoli florets to the water for the last five minutes of cooking.

Editor’s Tip: Here’s what al dente actually means, and how to achieve it in your fettuccine and other pastas.

Meanwhile, in a large skillet, cook the chicken and chopped onion in butter until the chicken is no longer pink. Add the minced garlic, salt and cayenne pepper, and cook for one minute longer. Stir in the flour until it’s blended with the other ingredients.

Gradually add the half-and-half, thawed peas and Parmesan cheese to the skillet. Bring the mixture to a boil. Cook and stir the sauce for one to two minutes or until it’s thickened.

Drain the fettuccine and broccoli, and toss them with the chicken mixture. Serve the chicken broccoli Alfredo while it’s hot.

Once the chicken broccoli Alfredo cools, transfer it to a sealed food storage container. Store it in the refrigerator for up to four days.

Yes, you can prepare this dish up to three days ahead of time. Gently reheat the chicken broccoli Alfredo in a covered skillet on the stove.

The creamy sauce in this Alfredo recipe may separate and turn watery when frozen and then thawed. To protect the texture, it’s best not to freeze chicken broccoli Alfredo.

Yes, you can substitute cubed chicken thighs for the chicken breast. Cook the thighs in butter until the internal temperature reaches 170°F.

Save a little time by using meat from a cooked rotisserie chicken. Cube or shred the breast meat—or a combination of breast and dark meat. Add the chicken to the sauce near the end of cooking time to warm it through.

Yes, frozen broccoli can be substituted for fresh. Add the frozen florets to the pasta water a couple of minutes before the end of cooking time to blanch them.

#6625. Triple Chocolate Mousse Cake

This chocolate mousse cake ticks a lot of boxes—big, grand, ideal for the holidays, and just enough of a challenge to ensure you feel accomplished. The one-bowl chocolate cake layer is dense and deeply fudgy; the mousse is airy and light; and the thin slip of ganache on top brings it all together. No matter what kind of year you’ve had, this dessert is the way to cap it all off.

Making the mousse alone will teach you three foundational pastry techniques, and they’re all hidden in plain sight. It starts with a crème anglaise; adding that to chopped chocolate yields a crémeux, and folding in whipped cream turns it into a mousse. Magical. The cake can be easily made from start to finish in the space of a morning, but can be split up further to fit your schedule. Bake the chocolate cake layer and chop all the chocolate on the first day; make the mousse and assemble the cake the following.

Welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep on why it works. Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack.

1 hour 30 minutes (plus 6 hours for chilling)

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Lay a sheet of parchment paper over base of pan. Fit band on top and clamp shut to hold parchment in place; scrunch up around base. Wrap a sheet of foil around bottom and up sides of pan (this will help prevent any leaking).

Whisk together 1 cup (125 g) all-purpose flour, 1 cup (200 g) sugar, ⅓ cup (28 g) Dutch-process cocoa powder, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. baking soda in a medium bowl. Add 1 large egg, ⅓ cup buttermilk, ⅓ cup vegetable oil, 1 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, and ½ cup water and whisk until smooth, about 1 minute. Scrape batter into prepared pan.

Bake cake until a tester inserted into the center comes out with a few moist crumbs attached and top springs back when gently pressed, 25–35 minutes. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let cake cool in pan 10 minutes. Remove band from base; slide cake off parchment and base and onto rack. Let cool completely; discard parchment and foil.

Do Ahead: Cake can be baked 1 day ahead. Store tightly wrapped at room temperature.

Place 10.5 oz. bittersweet chocolate, preferably 70% cacao, coarsely chopped, in a large heatproof bowl. Bring 1 cup whole milk to a simmer in a small saucepan over medium, about 5 minutes.

Meanwhile, vigorously whisk 4 large egg yolks and ½ cup (100 g) sugar in a small heatproof bowl until smooth and lemon yellow, about 1 minute.

Gradually stream hot milk into yolk mixture, whisking constantly until combined. Return to pan, scraping bowl clean with a heatproof rubber spatula. Cook over medium, stirring constantly, until thickened just enough to coat a spoon, about 5 minutes. (Do not let custard come to a boil or it will curdle.) Immediately pour over chocolate; let sit 1 minute. Add 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt and 1 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract and whisk vigorously until chocolate is melted and crémeux is smooth.

Beat 1¾ cups heavy cream in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment on medium speed until soft peaks form, about 5 minutes. Add one quarter of whipped cream to crémeux; mix until combined (this will lighten it). Add remaining whipped cream in 3 additions, gently folding after each until incorporated before adding more.

Reassemble springform pan; line bottom with a parchment paper round. Wrap a strip of parchment around inside of pan to create a collar that stands about 1" above band (ends should overlap by at least 3"). Using a large serrated knife, trim off mound on top of cake to create a flat surface if needed. Return cake to pan. Spoon mousse over and smooth into an even layer with an offset spatula or spoon. Place pan on a rimmed baking sheet; chill until top of mousse feels set, about 2 hours.

Place 4 oz. bittersweet chocolate, preferably 70% cacao, coarsely chopped, in a medium heatproof bowl. Bring ½ cup heavy cream and ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt to a bare simmer in a small saucepan over medium. Pour over chocolate and let sit 2 minutes. Whisk gently until smooth. If ganache feels hot, let cool until lukewarm but still pourable, 8–10 minutes.

Pour ganache over mousse and smooth with offset spatula. Chill until mousse is completely set (ganache will set in about 30 minutes), at least 4 hours and up to 12 hours (no need to cover unless fridge has other strong smells).

To serve, remove band from base and peel parchment strip away from sides of cake. Transfer cake with base to a plate and let sit 20 minutes; sprinkle top with flaky sea salt.

#6622. Maple-Sausage Breakfast Casserole

Inspired by the iconic egg and sausage sandwich on a pancake bun, this breakfast casserole is cheesy and just a smidge sweet from the brushing of maple butter at the very end. Destined for holiday brunch tables everywhere and best enjoyed while you’re still in pajamas, this cozy bake will feed a full house. (Don’t be surprised if you find yourself making it again long after the last guest leaves though!)

More high-protein breakfast recipes here.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 400°. Lightly coat a 13x9" baking dish with nonstick vegetable oil spray. Whisk 2½ cups (313 g) all-purpose flour, ¼ cup (50 g) sugar, 2 Tbsp. baking powder, 2 tsp. freshly ground pepper, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl to combine. Set aside.

Cook 2 lb. breakfast sausage, casings removed if needed, in a large skillet set over medium-high heat, stirring and breaking into small pieces with a wooden spoon, until browned and cooked through, 10–12 minutes. Using a slotted spoon, transfer sausage to a small plate, leaving fat behind. Pour fat into a heatproof measuring glass. You want ½ cup fat; spoon out any excess or pour in vegetable oil as needed if you don’t have enough. Stir 2 large eggs and 2 cups whole milk into fat. Let sausage cool slightly, then crumble into small, even pieces with your hands.

Pour fat mixture into reserved dry ingredients and stir until just combined and no large dry pockets of flour remain (batter may be thin and lumpy; it’ll be fine). Set aside ½ cup sausage and ½ cup cheese from 8 oz. sharp yellow cheddar, coarsely grated (about 2 cups), for topping, then add remaining sausage and cheddar to batter and stirring until evenly distributed.

Scrape batter into prepared baking dish and evenly scatter reserved sausage and cheese over. Bake casserole until top springs back when gently pressed with your finger and a tester inserted into the center comes out with just a few moist crumbs attached, 20–30 minutes.

Just before casserole is done, heat 2 Tbsp. pure maple syrup and 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a small skillet over medium, stirring occasionally, until butter is melted, about 2 minutes.

Brush maple butter over casserole and let cool 10 minutes. Cut into squares. Serve with more maple syrup and butter alongside.

#6621. Flashback to 1965: Truman Capote and the Seaside Studio He Designed for Work

“Truman Capote and the Country Studio He Designed for Work,” photographed by Horst P. Horst originally appeared in the November 1965 issue of Vogue.

For more of the best from Vogue’s archive, sign up for our Nostalgia newsletter here.

When Truman Capote, a resilient, gregarious man with a roaming, compassionate mind, leaves his extraordinarily worldly life, he has three ivory towers, his house in Brooklyn, his apartment in Verbier, Switzerland, and now his beach studio on Long Island. He designed that studio for work. There he finished the galleys of his new book, In Cold Blood, the brilliant, true story of the murder of a Kansas family. If he is not working, he likes the rich soft life, cruising the Mediterranean on a great yacht, visiting the famous houses of friends, dancing, playing, talking. One of the best conversationalists, he never mixes play and work. No nipping upstairs to write for an hour or so. At his beach house, he works for concentrated hours in a narrow, monastic office with only a table and a typewriter. Nothing distracts him. When he comes out, he takes pleasure in his plain, grey-brown wooden house, set down a few hundred yards from the ocean on a strip of moor between wheat and potato fields. The house, very like its owner, is straight-forward American, amusing, polished, with good proportions and an attractive shake of Capote charm; interesting because it is his.

Bright, shining colors are the mark of Truman Capote’s studio with its sophisticated farmhouse qualities. It fits Capote: witty, complicatedly simple, with extravagant gestures. After he bought the house, he had it stripped down to a shell, then converted it to his needs: a lot of color, the look of raw woods, comfort, a good kitchen, and no guest rooms. (When a friend came for lunch, he found Capote marinating cucumbers.) It is so solitary—the beach stretches four miles on either side of the house—that on the Fourth of July he saw only three people walking along.

Capote in the living room, partly double-storeyed. At his feet, an Andy Warhol portrait of Capote, painted 10 years earlier.

A lion-skin rug, given to Capote by Winston F. C. Guest who shot the lion, lies in the upstairs living room off the gallery. The extravagance: two living rooms for one man.

In the downstairs living room, a corner with a Tiffany glass lamp and part of a collection of French glass paperweights.

On the small dining room table (rarely any guests) a plate of tomatoes, lemons, and limes.

Against wallpaper patterned like Portuguese tiles hangs one of a pair of French 19th-century mirrors, formed like a butterfly.

In the master bedroom, the brass bed has a cover of woolwork, designed by Truman Capote, of yellow roses on a white background. (He found a rose in an old hat, had the rose copied for the pattern.)

Capote in his Jaguar XKE, painted a very dark green, the green, in fact, of Chinese holly. He is wearing his “disappearing hat,” a camouflage in green and white, with the front turned down, the back turned up.

#6619. Sticky Miso Chicken

Miso, soy, and honey are a powerful trio, creating a savory marinade that could make just about anything sing (cod or salmon, broccoli or zucchini, tofu). Do have a keen eye on your chicken (especially if you have a drawer-style broiler at the bottom of your oven), checking it every so often to prevent a completely blackened cook.

It’s That Simple is our series about recipes so easy, you can make them with your eyes closed. Think tiny ingredient lists, laid-back techniques, and results so delicious you’ll text home about them. Read more: My Go-To Marinade for Chicken Is 3 Ingredients.

Heat broiler. Whisk ¼ cup honey, ¼ cup white miso, and 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce in a large bowl to combine. Add 1½ lb. skinless, boneless chicken thighs (the miso and soy sauce are plenty salty, so no need to season the chicken) and toss to coat. Arrange on wire rack set inside a rimmed baking sheet lined with foil and spoon any marinade remaining in bowl over. Broil chicken, turning halfway through, until cooked through and deeply charred in spots, 10–15 minutes (keep a close eye on it). Thinly slice chicken. Serve over steamed white rice, topped with thinly sliced scallions, if desired.

#6617. HexClad Bakeware Review: This Set Is So Sturdy and Nonstick, I’m Ditching Parchment Paper

As an avid baker, I've been waiting for such a sturdy set.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

Serious bakers will appreciate the hefty, high-quality materials in this 6-piece set. It's also gloriously nonstick.

When I got married a few years ago, I put a cohesive bakeware set on my registry to replace years of mismatched Goodwill finds. While it worked well for a few months, within a year it began to show serious signs of wear and tear. Baked-on grease stains, rust spots and even warping had me in the market for a new bakeware set much sooner than I expected.

So, when I heard that my favorite cookware brand was releasing a bakeware set promising a sturdy, nonstick experience, I jumped at the chance to test it. Here’s everything you need to know about the new HexClad bakeware line, including my honest thoughts after two months of testing.

HexClad’s new hybrid bakeware set features six core pieces:

It merges the benefits of stainless steel and nonstick into one easy-to-clean package. HexClad’s “hybrid technology” combines hexagonal steel peaks with nonstick valleys to improve heat circulation and release after baking. In other words, this bakeware browns your food evenly without it sticking to the pan.

Other features include ergonomic handles and a 2.5mm tri-ply construction to prevent warping. It’s also oven-safe up to 900 degrees Fahrenheit and dishwasher-safe. You can even use your favorite metal spatula or tongs without scratching the surface. And, like all HexClad cookware, it comes with a lifetime warranty against manufacturer’s defects.

I’ll admit: I’m already a big fan of HexClad. I reach for the brand’s skillets and knives daily, and I’ve hoped for years that they would release a bakeware line.

So, when the offer to test the new set landed in my inbox, I couldn’t say no. But would it live up to the hype I’d built up in my head? I put all six pieces through the paces for two months to find out.

Like all HexClad products I’ve tried, the bakeware packaging experience is impeccable. The set arrived securely in one big box, separated with foam. Each piece was also wrapped in a protective dust bag, which is a nice touch.

Immediately, I was awed by the construction of these pans. Just by touch, I could tell they were high quality. I grabbed my food scale to compare the weight of the HexClad pans to my go-to carbon steel pans. The HexClad options weighed more than twice as much as my existing bakeware. Talk about heft!

Now, some folks might not appreciate that extra weight—especially since the pans get even heavier when full of food. But as someone who often replaces her bakeware every few years due to warping or rusting, I’m excited for a sturdier option. I hope this is the last set of bakeware I ever need to order.

As a final step, I washed each piece and got ready to bake!

One of my favorite things to make with sourdough discard is a big loaf of focaccia bread, so that was a natural first test in the 13×9 HexClad pan. Focaccia dough is sticky, but a generous coating of olive oil helps prevent it from gluing to the pan. Still, after proofing and baking my bread as usual, I was impressed that the final product pulled slightly away from the pan’s edges, making it slide out with complete ease. The bottom and edges got nice and toasty brown, too.

A few nights later, I used the same focaccia dough to make a focaccia pizza. Same sticky dough, made even stickier with tomato sauce, cheese and toppings. Plus, since it’s such a rich dish, I cut back on the amount of olive oil I used. Despite all the add-ons, this focaccia baked and released from the pan just as beautifully as the first loaf.

Next, I made a chocolate layer cake with the 9-inch round cake pans. Now, I’m typically a ride-or-die parchment paper user. I find cutting out perfectly sized parchment circles a tedious task, but it’s worthwhile insurance against my cakes sticking. But to truly put the HexClad pans’ nonstick properties to the test, I skipped adding parchment and simply greased my pans with a little butter and flour.

After baking and 10 minutes of cooling came the moment of truth: Would it stick? Luckily, no! Both cakes released with minimal effort. I simply ran a butter knife around the rim of the cake before using the cooling rack to flip ’em out. It’s a good thing, too, because this was my dad’s birthday cake!

My nonstick tests continued with the 8×8 square pan when I whipped up a batch of candy bar blondies. These blondies used an assortment of leftover Halloween candy, so I thought for sure the caramel ooze from a Baby Ruth bar would cause some issues. But nope! Even without parchment paper, treats slipped right out of the pan.

But how does HexClad bakeware perform with healthier treats? For one final test, I baked a completely made-up “brownie” recipe with pumpkin seed butter, applesauce, molasses and cocoa. It was a gooey, chocolaty mess by the time I put it in the pan, yet it baked and released beautifully.

Finally, I put the baking sheet to the test.

Now, I already own the HexClad pizza steel, which I use almost daily. It’s my go-to for everything from frozen pizza to galettes to roasted broccoli, and I find that it works even better than an air fryer to yield crisp, golden brown bakes. I’ve said on many occasions that it’s my all-time favorite piece of bakeware, especially for savory foods.

Both the pizza steel and baking sheet utilize HexClad’s tri-ply construction with an aluminum core and TerraBond nonstick coating. The former is a jet black colorway, while the baking sheet is gray.

Across the board, I found the baking sheet could handle every task I threw its way—including roasting a spaghetti squash. Oftentimes, I find myself scrubbing for what feels like days after roasting squash and scouring off that sticky, burnt-on residue. The HexClad pan cleaned with a simple swipe from a damp paper towel.

During testing, I found the bottoms and handles of the HexClad bakeware smudged a bit. After all, it is made of stainless steel. This didn’t bother me, and it was easy to clean by handwashing and drying it immediately. Over time, I may need to use a more abrasive regimen to clean stainless steel.

While the HexClad pans are very sturdy, you should still let them fully cool before washing. Don’t throw a hot pan directly in the sink. The pans are also dishwasher-safe, though handwashing is recommended. (And honestly, so easy thanks to the nonstick coating.)

Across the board, I’m impressed with the new HexClad bakeware line. I hope we see even more pieces in the future, like a muffin tin and loaf pan. Only time will tell exactly how it holds up, but from what I’ve experienced so far, this set really is designed to last a lifetime. (And I’ll be continuing to long-term test the set, and update this review accordingly.)

Ready to take your bakes to the next level? This all-in-one set is great for beginners and pros alike.

You can shop the full 6-piece bakeware set on the HexClad website for $399. Select styles, like 2-pack sets of small and medium baking sheets, are also available.

#6616. The Tucson Restaurant Turning Cactus Into Fine Dining

Traipsing through Tucson Mountain Park, a Midwestern blow-in might not identify much to eat. Plants armed with burs, barbs, and spines all but scream “do not touch.” For chef Aaron Lopez and June Chee, however, this prickly, dusty landscape stocks a pantry of possibility. The married co-owners of Ursa see the Arizona desert as a rich ground for foraging.

Gray, tangled brittlebush, which the average Tucsonan walks or drives by almost daily, can be pressure-cooked, caramelized until black, and baked into cake. Dusty, sage-colored salt bush, when hung to dry, takes on an intensely umami, aquatic saltiness like seaweed. The sweet buds of the Seussian-green palo verde tree become briny, like olives, when suffused with lye.

Don’t even get Lopez started on the dozens of cacti varieties that thrive here, which the restaurant sources from local grower Toadlet Farm and which Lopez harvests throughout the year. The restaurant processes the young and mature paddles, fruit and their seeds, buds, and flowers, which are then grilled, poached, cold-smoked, juiced, dehydrated, nixtamalized, or preserved into jam, wine, and vinegar.

There are hundreds of edible plants in the Sonoran Desert. Ursa strives to showcase their potential, one 10-course meal at a time.

“We treat Ursa as an art showroom, demonstrating to people what these plants can do, what sustainable means, and what was here before it got easy,” says Lopez. The idea was inspired in part by his Sonoran grandfather, Hector Lopez, who died in the spring. “He was the first person I ever heard say they’re proud to be from the desert,” the chef said.

Ursa began as a pop-up in El Centro, California, in 2023. Lopez and Chee moved to a historic brick building in downtown Tucson, re-opening their doors in October 2025. It’s a homecoming of sorts for the couple, who are both from the Sonoran Desert borderlands. They met in Hawaii, where Chee was working in clean energy and transportation. Lopez, meanwhile, spent roughly 18 years cooking in fine dining and modern progressive restaurants like Redbird and Orsa & Winston in LA, and Pai Honolulu. But he was longing for the desert.

After helping a friend open a restaurant and hosting a few popups in Austin, Lopez and Chee bought a desert foraging guide, packed up their two dogs and began driving around the Southwest. It made sense to settle in Tucson, which was recognized by UNESCO in 2015 as a Creative City of Gastronomy for its continuous 4,000-year agricultural history and deeply rooted Sonoran Desert food traditions.

“That’s a unique thing about being here, the connection from seed to plant to restaurant that we hadn’t been able to grasp before,” Chee says.

Consider a recent course that Ursa built around tepary beans, in which the ancient, nutty bean is refried and topped with h:al squash that’s been lactofermented. The squash’s leaves are fermented to make Japanese-style kosho and its flowers are pickled, dried, crushed with dried saltbush, then tossed with barrel cactus seeds for a desert furikake. It’s served with grilled coins of chorizo made from Lopez’s great-grandmother’s recipe and housemade flour tortillas, to all be washed down with an amazake drink made from fermented wheat and goat fat. Don’t get too attached, however. Riffs owing to finicky ingredient availability occur here almost daily.

Running a restaurant using only ingredients foraged and farmed from within about eight to 10 miles means abiding by pretty intense guardrails. The only wheat used is pima club, an ancient soft white variety cultivated for centuries by the Akimel O’odham (Pima) people. Ursa does not use cucumbers, radishes or citrus.

“We’re not trying to substitute anything, like, ‘How do we achieve cucumber? Let’s grab a cactus,’” Lopez says. “We have to throw everything out, really strip it down. Sometimes we have to let the ingredients be bitter or spicy. We have to put our egos aside and let the ingredient be the star.”

For staff who didn’t grow up or learn to cook here, the learning curve at Ursa can feel a little like alighting on a new planet, even if certain flora happen to resemble prickly weeds in their own backyards.

“We have these really cool moments in the restaurant where people are like, Oh! I have lamb’s quarter just growing in my yard!” Chee says of the spinach-like desert green that appears all over Ursa’s menu.

A young Aaron Lopez with his grandfather Hector Lopez.

Ursa’s approach isn’t always easy for customers to understand, so the couple came up with a more down-to-earth option. This fall, the restaurant debuted a four-course, family-style Lineage menu for $75, alongside the existing 10-course Harvest menu ($150). There’s now a pozole course inspired by the family’s annual springtime tradition of roasting goat in agave leaves, barbacoa-style, and shredding it for soup, and a red masa tamal with glazed quail and yucca blossoms in mole made with burnt mesquite bread, a technique Lopez remembers from childhood.

The idea took shape during Ursa’s extended summer break, as Lopez recovered from foot surgery and reflected on the loss of his late grandfather, the tenacious keeper of family traditions.

“I feel so much closer to my ancestors and the land; we want Ursa to be less esoteric and more soulful,” he says. “The story of Ursa is partly of the desert, partly my family. Now we’ve advanced to the point where they’re symbiotic, and I can't tell them apart.”

#6615. Anchovy-Garlic Pasta

Even those who swear they don’t like anchovies should be willing to take a “no thank-you” portion of this pasta. Sizzled with garlic, the tiny fish melt into a briny sauce that’s similar to bagna cauda, the warm Northern Italian dip whose savory quality comes from said anchovies. Instead of serving alongside crudités, toss this sauce with hot long pasta like linguine or spaghetti. No extra vegetables or protein needed, but I wouldn’t kick a salad with beans and bitter-slanting greens (kale, radicchio) off the table.

More weeknight-friendly pasta dinners this way.

Cook fillets and oil from two 2-oz. tins oil-packed anchovy fillets, ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil, and ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper in a large high-sided skillet or medium Dutch oven over medium-low heat, breaking up fillets with a wooden spoon or heatproof rubber spatula, until anchovies are melted and mixture is bubbling, about 2 minutes. Add 6 garlic cloves, finely grated, and cook, stirring often, until fragrant, about 30 seconds. Remove pan from heat.

Cook 12 oz. long pasta (such as linguine or spaghetti) in a large pot of boiling salted water until very al dente, about 3 minutes less than package directions. Drain, reserving 2 cups pasta cooking liquid.

Gradually pour 1 cup pasta cooking liquid into anchovy mixture in pan, whisking constantly to incorporate. Place pan over high heat and bring sauce to a simmer. Add pasta and cook, tossing vigorously with tongs, until pasta is al dente and sauce is slightly thickened, about 2 minutes.

Remove pasta from heat and add 3 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, cut into pieces. Toss until butter is melted and pasta is coated and glossy, about 45 seconds. Add 1 cup coarsely chopped parsley, 1 Tbsp. finely grated lemon zest, and 3 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice and toss to combine, adding more pasta cooking liquid a splash at a time as needed to keep pasta saucy. Divide among shallow bowls to serve.

#6613. Is Pink Turkey Safe to Eat?

Pink turkey doesn't necessarily mean your Thanksgiving feast is ruined. Here's how to know if your bird is safe to eat so you can stay calm and turkey on.

I’ll never forget the Thanksgiving when I was convinced I’d ruined the holiday for everyone. I wasn’t an experienced cook at the time, and it was one of my first attempts at making a Thanksgiving turkey. I used a helpful guide for how long to cook a turkey and even invested in a meat thermometer to be sure it reached at least 165°F. It looked great, and I was so proud!

Imagine my surprise and horror when I carved that gorgeously browned roast turkey and discovered it was pink inside. I was so nervous my guests would assume the turkey was undercooked. I didn’t know then that pink turkey can be perfectly safe to eat—as long as it’s cooked to that vital internal temperature.

Cooked turkey can look pink for a few reasons that have nothing to do with doneness, including the age of the bird, how it’s prepared and natural pigmentation.

“Poultry naturally can have a pink hue,” says Heidi Diestel of turkey farm Diestel Family Ranch in Sonora, California. “The legs and thighs have more of the natural pigments that give meat its darker color. Those pigments, along with changes that happen during cooking, can leave some pink even when the turkey is fully cooked.”

The pigments Heidi refers to are proteins called myoglobin and cytochrome c. The more of these proteins the meat has, the darker it will be. Older animals tend to have more proteins, and therefore darker pigmentation, as do any regularly exercised muscles. That explains why leg meat is darker than breast meat, as turkeys spend the bulk of their days walking and running.

Cooking can also cause a chemical reaction with these proteins that contributes to a pink color. Smoked turkey often stays pink from the reaction of the meat to the smoke inside the grill or smoker, but even oven-roasted turkey can have a pinkish hue. Myoglobin usually turns white during the cooking process, but cytochrome c is more resistant to heat and can maintain a pink blush.

Using a meat thermometer is the best way to know if your turkey is safe to eat.

Poultry is considered safe to eat when it meets a cooking temperature of at least 165°. However, the Taste of Home Test Kitchen recommends cooking the leg and thigh meat to 170° for the best texture. For stuffed turkeys, don’t forget to take the temperature of the stuffing as well, which should reach at least 165° when the thermometer is inserted in the center of the stuffing.

If your turkey comes embedded with a round plastic doneness indicator that pops when the turkey is ready, don’t use that as an absolute; they are notoriously inaccurate.

To check if the turkey is done, insert the thermometer in a thick, meaty area, making sure the tip doesn’t touch any bones (bone will show a higher temperature).

If you’re using a probe thermometer that you insert before cooking, double-check its position once the turkey has been cooking for a while. Meat contracts as it cooks, so it may no longer be in the best spot.

If any part of your turkey is below 165°, you should continue cooking the turkey until all parts reach a safe temperature. It’s common for the thermometer to register different temperatures in different areas, since white meat cooks at a faster rate than dark meat. Don’t be tempted to cut off the parts that aren’t ready and return only them to the oven. It’ll increase the risk that undercooked juices will run onto your cutting board and contaminate the properly cooked turkey.

If the legs and thighs aren’t done but the breast is, I like to baste the white meat and loosely tent it with foil to try and lock in as much moisture as possible. If the dark meat is ready but the breast needs more time, there’s no need to sweat it. Dark meat has enough natural fat and moisture that it won’t become dry with a little extra time in the oven.

You should never knowingly eat undercooked turkey. According to the CDC, undercooked turkey can contain harmful bacteria, like Salmonella, Clostridium perfringens or Campylobacter, that can cause foodborne illnesses.

There’s also a risk of bacteria if the turkey isn’t thawed or prepared correctly. Give yourself plenty of time to thaw a frozen turkey, either in the refrigerator or in a cold water bath. Also, make sure to keep the counter or cutting board where you’re prepping the turkey clean and sanitized before and after handling the raw bird.
